'''Arduaine''' ({{langx|gd|An Àird Uaine|translation=green/fertile promontory or headland}}, pronounced ''"Ar-DOO-nee"'') is a Scottish coastal hamlet located on the A816 about 20 miles south of Oban and 18 miles north of Lochgilphead. It is in the council area of [[Argyll and Bute Council|Argyll and Bute]], at the southern boundary of the civil parish of Kilmelford and Kilninver, and comprises about two dozen houses, a hotel and restaurant, and a botanical garden.

The settlement was originally named Asknish, but tea planter J. Arthur Campbell was required to change the name when he bought the estate in 1897 (the previous owners of the estate then started using the name [[Asknish]] for the Lochgair mansion house that their predecessors had built in the late 18th century).

==History==
===Iron Age===
The earliest known settlement in Arduaine is evidenced by the ruins of a late prehistoric [[Dun (fortification)|dun]] on the headland, the name of which is given as Dungaivlaig on the mid-18th century [[William Roy|Roy's map]].<ref>
{{Cite web
|url=https://maps.nls.uk/geo/roy/#zoom=15.0&lat=56.23780&lon=-5.55966&layers=roy-highlands
|title=Roy's Map
|accessdate=16 June 2025}}
</ref> Excavation of the site in 2011 failed to find any artefacts that might enable accurate dating.<ref>
{{Cite web
|url=https://www.trove.scot/place/22619#:~:text=Excavation%20(21st%20April-,2011,-%2D%2029th%20April%202011
|title=Dungaivlaig on trove.scot
|accessdate=16 June 2025}}
</ref>  It is likely that the area was inhabited prior to the Iron Age too, as there is a Bronze Age cist at Degnish <ref>
{{Cite web
|url=https://www.trove.scot/place/22624
|title=Degnish cist on trove.scot
|accessdate=16 June 2025}}
</ref> (opposite Arduaine on the other side of the mouth of Loch Melfort), and a cave on the southern slope of An Sidhean ("Fairy Hill") near Kilmelford was found to contain Stone Age artefacts.<ref>
{{Cite web
|url=https://www.trove.scot/place/22882
|title=An Sidhean cave, Kilmelford on trove.scot
|accessdate=16 June 2025}}
</ref>

There are dozens of ruined duns in the local area, the next nearest ones to Arduaine being:

* a D-shaped possible promontory fort at Creag Aoil (“Lime Rock”),<ref>
{{Cite web
|url=https://www.trove.scot/place/22880
|title=Creag Aoil dun, Kames on trove.scot
|accessdate=16 June 2025}}
</ref> a small headland about 1km NE of Arduaine further along the south coast of Loch Melfort.

* Dun Fadaidh (“Kindling Fort”) at Degnish.<ref>
{{Cite web
|url=https://www.trove.scot/place/?
|title=Dun Fadaidh, Degnish on trove.scot
|accessdate=16 June 2025}}
</ref>

* a 53m by 28m pear-shaped fort dated to around 300BC at Eilean An Duin ("Fort Island"),<ref>
{{Cite web
|url=https://www.trove.scot/place/22536
|title=Eilean An Duin, Craobh Haven on trove.scot
|accessdate=16 June 2025}}
</ref> one of the Craobh Islands now connected to the mainland by a causeway near [[Craobh Haven]] marina.

* a galleried dun at Caisteal Nan Coin Duibh (“Castle of the Black Dogs”) on the northwest slopes of Mullach Dubh (“Black Hilltop”) near Craobh Haven.<ref>
{{Cite web
|url=https://www.trove.scot/place/22744
|title=Caisteal Nan Coin Duibh, Craobh Haven on trove.scot
|accessdate=16 June 2025}}
</ref>

===Middle Ages===
The local duns may have served various purposes, such as dwellings or meeting places, beacons or watchtowers, at different stages of the area's history. There have certainly been some turbulent periods when they could have formed useful parts of the area's maritime defences, for example:

* Romans [[Roman conquest of Britain|did not settle locally]] but perhaps tried raiding the area for slaves from the 1st to 3rd centuries.<ref>Tacitus, Cornelius (1854) [98], "The Life of Cnaeus Julius Agricola", The Works of Tacitus (The Oxford Translation, Revised), vol. II, London: Henry G. Bohn, pp. 343–389</ref>
* There were 4th century raids by the Irish, who subsequently colonised Argyll and established the 5th to 8th century Kingdom of [[Dál Riata|Dalriada]].<ref>Charles-Edwards, T. M., 'The Britons and the Irish, 350–800', Wales and the Britons, 350-1064 (Oxford, 2012; online edn, Oxford Academic, 24 Jan. 2013), https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198217312.003.0005, accessed 21 June 2025.</ref> During this period, Asknish would have formed part of the tribal lands controlled by the [[Cenél Loairn|Cenel Loairn]] (whose name persists as the district of Lorn).<ref>Pahl, Katrina, "CENEL LOAIRN, CENEL nGABRAIN & THE MYSTERY OF MORAY" (2024). Regis University Student Publications (comprehensive collection). 1138. https://epublications.regis.edu/theses/1138</ref>
* Dalriada itself then suffered 9th century raids by the [[Vikings]], who subsequently colonised the outer and [[Inner Hebrides]] and established the 9th to 13th century Norse “[[Kingdom of the Isles]]”.<ref>Woolf, Alex. From Pictland to Alba, 789-1070. Edinburgh University Press, 2007. pp. 95–96</ref> The Norse origin of the name Asknish (“Ash(tree)" + "ness/headland”)<ref>The place-names of Argyll
by Gillies, H. Cameron, Publication date 1906, p222 https://archive.org/details/placenamesofargy00gill/page/222/mode/2up?q=asknish</ref> suggests it may have been part of or at least on the borders of that territory.

===13th to 18th century===
From 1222 onwards Asknish was a lairdship of the [[Clan MacIver|MacIvers of Lergachonzie]] (Lergachonzie being the old name of current farmland and holiday cottages at Lergychoniebeg and Lergychoniemor just to the south of Arduaine; the name perhaps derives from leargaidh-còinnich, or "mossy slopes"). The MacIvers were apparently granted these lands in return for their allegiance to Alexander II (King of Alba) during the 1221–22 [[Scottish expedition into Argyll (1221–1222)|subjugation of Argyll]].<ref>Argyll, House of. The House of Argyll and the Collateral Branches of the Clan Campbell, from the Year 420 to the Present Time. [With a Portrait and a Genealogical Table.]. Glasgow: J. Tweed, 1871. P172 https://digital.nls.uk/95554337</ref>

The early MacIver family's main seat is likely to have been Dun An Garbh-Sroine (“Fort of the Rocky Knoll”), a now ruined 84m by 34m rectangular fort (which would have been one of the largest forts in Argyll) near Garraron Farm about 1km south of Arduaine.<ref>
{{Cite web
|url=https://www.trove.scot/place/22739
|title=Dun An Garbh-Sroine, Garraron on trove.scot
|accessdate=16 June 2025}}
</ref>
The MacIvers allied with [[Clan Campbell]] and this fort could have been an important defence against coastal attacks on the Campbell powerbases further inland at Loch Awe.

The MacIvers later chose or were compelled to use the name MacIver Campbell, or simply Campbell; and after the lands of Lergachonzie were given as a dowry in the 17th century, they assumed the territorial designation “of Asknish”.<ref>Argyll, House of. The House of Argyll and the Collateral Branches of the Clan Campbell, from the Year 420 to the Present Time. [With a Portrait and a Genealogical Table.]. Glasgow: J. Tweed, 1871. P175 https://digital.nls.uk/95554373</ref>
The last male heir of the original MacIver of Lergachonzie chief was Robert Campbell of Asknish,<ref>Argyll, House of. [https://digital.nls.uk/95554409 "The House of Argyll and the Collateral Branches of the Clan Campbell, from the Year 420 to the Present Time. [With a Portrait and a Genealogical Table"]. Glasgow: J. Tweed, 1871. P175</ref> who built himself a mansion house on an estate he bought near Lochgair in 1768.<ref>Campbell, and Campbell, Peter Colin. An Account of the Clan-Iver. Aberdeen: P.C. Campbell, 1873. P43 https://digital.nls.uk/95352551</ref>

===19th century===
{{overly detailed|section|date=April 2026}}
On Robert Campbell's death, his properties including Lochgair House and the Asknish estate passed initially to Duncan Paterson (whose predecessor had married Robert Campbell's sister Agnes), and later to Aylmer Vivian (who had married Duncan Paterson's daughter Margaret); however, on taking possession of their inheritance both the Paterson and Vivian families adopted the surname MacIver Campbell, perhaps hoping to bathe in the clan's reflected glory.<ref>Multiple sources:
* 1841 Scotland Census. Parish: Glassary; ED: 4; Page: 15; Line: 390; Year: 1841 - records “Duncan Campbell P” living with his sister “Amelia C Paterson” Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/
* 1851 Scotland Census. Parish: Glassary; ED: 6; Page: 15; Line: 9; Roll: CSSCT1851_109; Year: 1851 - records “Duncan C Paterson” living with his sister “Amelia Campbell Paterson” Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/
* 1861 Scotland Census. Parish: Glassary; ED: 6; Page: 14; Line: 1; Roll: CSSCT1861_70 - records “D Mc Iver Campbell Esq” living with his sister “Amelea Campbell” Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/
* 1871 Scotland Census. Parish: Glassary; ED: 6; Page: 14; Line: 1; Roll: CSSCT1871_90 - records “Duncan Campbell” living with his wife Elizabeth, brother Irwin, sister Amelia, and cousin Susan. Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/
* 1901 Scotland Census. Parish: Glassary; ED: 6; Page: 8; Line: 4; Roll: CSSCT1901_179 - records “Ayloner Mac Iver Campbell” with family and servants at the property now named “Lochgair Asknish House” Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/</ref>
They lived at Lochgair House while [[tenant farmer]]s at Asknish and other estates provided them with an income.

Census data indicates there were between three and five households in Asknish in the 19th century, apparently the main farmhouse and two to four farmworkers’ cottages. The occupant records for the main farmhouse provide a glimpse of what mid-19th century life was like:

1841 – The head of household is Duncan McPherson who is living with his wife Isabella (née McDougall, whose death records her as an illegitimate daughter of Colin McDougall, landed proprietor of Lunga<ref>Statutory Deaths in the District of Kilmore & Kilbride, 1900 https://www.ancestry.co.uk/mediaui-viewer/collection/1030/tree/203970138/media/41320e87-09ce-47d4-a0da-6dbfb9d204d3 Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/</ref>), along with four children under 8, and two farm servants.<ref>1841 Scotland Census. Parish: Kilninver; ED: 7; Page: 2; Line: 1340; Year: 1841 Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/</ref>

1851 – Isabella is now remarried to Duncan Campbell, and lives with him and seven children aged between 2 and 16 (five from her previous marriage and two with her new husband), and two servants. Duncan Campbell's occupation is given as “Farmer of 40 acres employing 2 labourers”.<ref>1851 Scotland Census. Parish: Kilninver; ED: 3; Page: 8; Line: 2; Roll: CSSCT1851_111; Year: 1851 Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/</ref>

1861 – Isabella's eldest son Duncan McPherson is now head of the Asknish farm household,<ref>Scotland Census 1861. Parish: Kilninver and Kilmelfort; ED: 2; Page: 1; Line: 1; Roll: CSSCT1861_70 Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/</ref> and Duncan and Isabella Campbell have moved to nearby Lergiechoniebeg West (with Duncan Campbell's occupation described there as “Farmer of 80 acres employing 1 boy”).<ref>1861 Scotland Census. Parish: Craignish; ED: 1; Page: 4; Line: 15; Roll: CSSCT1861_69 Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/</ref> Duncan McPherson is a “Farmer of 30 acres” and he shares Asknish with three of his sisters (one as housekeeper, one as a dairymaid and one described as “Shipmaster’s Wife”), two half-siblings who are still at school, two nephews and two farm servants (a shepherd and a ploughman).

1871 – Duncan McPherson has now moved to 12 Argyll Square and working as an innkeeper (still with his sister as housekeeper, and three half-siblings).<ref>Scotland Census 1871. Parish: Kilmore and Kilbride; ED: 2; Page: 8; Line: 16; Roll: CSSCT1871_91 Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/</ref> The new inhabitants of the main Asknish farmhouse are most likely John Crawford (a “shepherd”) and family <ref>Scotland Census 1871. Parish: Kilninver and Kilmelfort; ED: 2; Page: 10; Line: 1; Roll: CSSCT1871_91 Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/</ref> – although the name Asknish does not appear in the census record itself, John Crawford is named as occupier of Asknish in the Argyll Ordnance Survey Name Books at the time.<ref>https://scotlandsplaces.gov.uk/digital-volumes/ordnance-survey-name-books/argyll-os-name-books-1868-1878/argyll-volume-53/185 Accessed 23 June 2025 at https://www.ancestry.co.uk/</ref>

===20th century===
In 1897, tea planter J. Arthur Campbell bought the Asknish estate from Aylmer Vivian, then known as Colonel Aylmer MacIver Campbell of Lochgair. Arthur Campbell renamed the Asknish estate as “Arduaine” and started to replace the old Asknish farmhouse with a new house for his family, while Colonel MacIver Campbell began using the name Asknish for his Lochgair mansion.

Arthur Campbell's new Arduaine house was sold by his grandson to hoteliers in 1967 and is now the [[Loch Melfort Hotel]] and Restaurant; the house's nearby botanical garden, now known as Arduaine Garden, was sold separately in 1971 and eventually gifted to National Trust Scotland in 1992.

The settlement of Arduaine grew significantly in size in the mid-20th century, with one of the first additions being a shop and post office known as Arduaine Stores at the foot of Beinn Chaorach overlooking the newly built Arduaine Jetty. A caravan and camping site was created on the shore to the north of the jetty, and from the 1970s onwards several parcels of land near the shop were sold off as building plots, mostly for private residences but also including a cafe known as Arduaine Tearooms that was built with grants from the Highlands and Islands Development Board. However, by the end of the 20th century both the post office and cafe had closed and been converted to holiday homes; the caravan site had also closed and was in the process of being divided into three building plots for the private residences now seen there.

==Transport & Amenities==
Arduaine is on the 23 and 423 bus route <ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.westcoastmotors.co.uk/services/WCMO/423|title=423 - Ardrishaig to Oban|website=www.westcoastmotors.co.uk}}</ref> along the A816 between Oban and Ardrishaig.

Arduaine Jetty is the "ferry terminal" for the private boats taking holidaymakers to and from the cottages on the privately owned island of [[Shuna, Slate Islands|Shuna]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.islandofshuna.co.uk/index.html|title=Shuna Farm Cottages - Home Page|website=www.islandofshuna.co.uk}}</ref> as well as a launch point for sea kayak tours,<ref>https://www.wildaboutargyll.co.uk/see-and-do/on-in-the-water/argyll-sea-kayak-trail/</ref> paddle-boarders, divers and wild swimmers. There is a dedicated carpark next to the jetty for the vehicles supporting the sea kayak tours.

Asknish Bay also has a handful of buoy moorings mostly used by hotel and restaurant guests visiting by yacht.

Other amenities include a postbox, red telephone box (scheduled for decommissioning in 2025), glass bottle recycling banks and a waste skip.

==Geography==
Arduaine is a coastal hamlet most of which overlooks Asknish Bay, a horseshoe-shaped sea inlet which lies at the northeastern end of Loch Shuna. A geologic spit on the south side of Arduaine Point points to the rocky intertidal reef Eich Donna ("Brown Horses""), a formation which rises again further south as Eilean Creagach ("Craggy Island"). Eilean Gamhna ("Bullock Island") lies just off the west of Arduaine  Point, and Loch Melfort is to the north (some older maps refer to this southern end of Loch Melfort as North Asknish Bay). To the east of Arduaine the land rises steeply to a line of three successively higher peaks: Beinn Chaorach (“Sheepy Hill”), Càrn Dearg (“Red Ridge”) and Tom Solleir (“Shining Mount”). On [[William Roy|Roy's map]] this hilly moorland is labelled “Slientime”,<ref>https://maps.nls.uk/geo/roy/#zoom=15.0&lat=56.23449&lon=-5.52735&layers=0</ref> a name no longer in use and of unknown etymology.

==Folklore==
An Cnap - the hillock which rises in the middle of Arduaine Point - is referenced as Cnap-Aisginis ("Asknish Hill") by William Mackenzie in his 1895 collection of Gaelic incantations, which describes a ritual intended to cure ulcerous swellings of the armpit by chanting the names of specific local hills;<ref>{{cite book |last1=William |first1=Mackenzie |title=GAELIC INCANTATIONS CHARMS AND BLESSINGS OF THE HEBRIDES |date=1895 |page=68 |url=https://deriv.nls.uk/dcn23/1066/9761/106697618.23.pdf}}</ref> the idea is that the patient's swelling gets magically apportioned between those hills. In one example of the incantation collected on Colonsay, the names of twenty-seven local hills are recited, including "So air Mam Aisginis" ("This [part of the swelling apportioned] to Asknish Hill").

==Notable Residents==
[[Brigadier]] [[Sir]] [[Bruce Atta Campbell]] 2nd of Arduaine, {{post-nominals|country=GBR|size=100%|KCB|CBE|TD}} (1888{{snd}}1954), a British Army officer appointed as [[Lord Lieutenant of Argyllshire]] in 1949. He was Arthur Campbell's eldest son and lived in Arduaine House after the death of his mother Ethel in 1936.

==Arduaine Gardens==
Arduaine is home to the Arduaine Gardens which are in the care of the [[National Trust for Scotland]] and listed on the [[Inventory of Gardens and Designed Landscapes in Scotland]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.scottish-places.info/towns/townfirst553.html|title=Kilmelford: Overview|work=Gazetteer for Scotland|accessdate=27 December 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Historic Environment Scotland|num=GDL00025 |desc=ARDUAINE GARDENS |access-date=28 February 2019}}</ref>

12181409.title: Geilston Garden
12181409.extract:
Geilston Garden is a property of the National Trust for Scotland, north-west of Cardross, Argyll and Bute.
Geilston Garden was developed more than two hundred years ago with a date given for its development being 1797, combining several features (traditional walled garden, kitchen garden, wooded area). The walled garden has a dominating 100-foot Wellingtonia (Sequoiadendron giganteum) in the centre of the lawn. The Geilston burn wends its way through the north of the estate towards the River Clyde in Cardross. The origins of the garden were most likely a result of the 1770 Montgomery Act, which saw the land around the house enclosed and planting undertaken.
Geilston was opened to the public with the death of the last resident, Margaret Bell, who was a friend of Elizabeth Hendry, the owner of Geilston who bequeathed the house to the National trust for Scotland and gave her friend life rent of the house. The Hendrys moved into Geilston as tenants but the family bought the house from the Geils in 1922. The garden as it appears today was mostly laid out by Elizabeth Hendry and Margaret Bell. A cannon within the garden is said to have been a trophy from the Battle of Corunna brought to the Garden by Major General Geils, a previous owner of Geilston.
The kitchen garden is the most labour-intensive area. It springs to life in April with the first sowings of carrots, parsnips and beetroot closely followed by transplanted brassicas. Visitors can buy in-season produce from a small stand at the garden's entrance.
The walled garden is the focus of spring colour with azaleas, heathers and unusual shrubs such as Cornus kousa 'Satomi'. Summer colour is provided by the spectacularly vigorous species in the long herbaceous border – Thalictrum, Filipendula, Eupatorium, Helenium, Phlox and Sidalcea dominate the display.
The garden is open from April to October daily. The adjacent Geilston House is not open to the public.

Bucinch or Buc-Innis (Scottish Gaelic: "Buck Island" or "Male Goat Island") is a small island in Loch Lomond, in west central Scotland.
The heavily wooded island lies due north of Inchcruin and rises steeply from a rocky coastline to 24 metres (79 feet) in a central summit.
Along with smaller neighbour, Ceardach, Bucinch was donated to the National Trust for Scotland by Col Charles L Spencer of Warmanbie, Dumfries, in 1943. Although uninhabited for centuries, there are remains of a stone jetty.

Ceardach may have been the site of an Iron Age bloomery or furnace for smelting iron ore.<ref name="islands"/>

24028596.extract: Barry Mill is a working Category A listed watermill in Barry, Angus in eastern Scotland. It is owned and operated by the National Trust for Scotland as an educational tourist attraction. Situated in a secluded area beside the Barry Burn (the watercourse, which provides its power), the mill lies about half a mile north of the village of Barry, near the town of Carnoustie. A site for several mills since at least 1539, Barry Mill was commercially operational until 1984; it was then restored, and has been operated by the Trust since 1992. It was threatened with closure in March 2009, but has remained open due to local support, and the securing of external funding.

'''Barry Mill''' is a working [[listed building|Category A listed]] [[watermill]] in [[Barry, Angus|Barry]], [[Angus, Scotland|Angus]] in eastern [[Scotland]]. It is owned and operated by the [[National Trust for Scotland]] as an educational tourist attraction. Situated in a secluded area beside the [[Barry Burn]]<ref name="nts"/> (the watercourse, which provides its power), the mill lies about half a mile north of the village of Barry, near the town of [[Carnoustie]]. It is a three floor building, containing a meal floor (basement), a milling floor and a top (or "bin floor").<ref>[[#refZealand1992|Zealand & Zealand 1992]], p. 2.</ref> A site for several mills since at least 1539, Barry Mill was commercially operational until 1984; it was then restored, and has been operated by the Trust since 1992. It was threatened with closure in March 2009, but has remained open due to local support, and the securing of external funding.

==Operation==
[[File:Barry Mill Bridge.jpg|200px|thumb|right|Barry Burn]]
[[File:Barry Millstones.JPG|200px|thumb|left|Sandstone millstones]]
When in operation, the mill processes [[oat]]s into [[oatmeal]]. (Oatmeal being a staple foodstuff, that in the past commonly formed part of the basic diet in Scotland.<ref>Indeed, in the 1770s, on visiting Scotland, the English author [[Samuel Johnson]] wrote of oats as "a grain which in England is generally given to horses, but in Scotland supports the people." - ''The Life of Samuel Johnson'' by James Boswell, New York, 1858. Vol 3, p.11</ref>) Originally, the oats arrived in sacks from the neighbouring farms and had already been [[threshing|threshed]]. (There is an example of traditional threshing machine on display at the mill.) The oats were then dried in the mill's peat-fired [[kiln]] and then sent down a chute to the meal floor to be collected in sacks again. Today the oats arrive already processed, but the rest of the milling continues in the traditional style.<ref>[[#refZealand1992|Zealand & Zealand 1992]], p. 6.</ref>  
[[File:Barry Mill3.jpg|200px|thumb|right|The cog pit, showing the pit wheel (left), great spur wheel and a stone nut.]]
The oats are hoisted to the bin floor at the top of the mill, from where they are emptied into a hopper that feeds one of the mill's two pairs of [[millstone]]s situated on the mill floor. This pair of sandstone millstones shells the grain, and the output is then sent down a chute to the basement where the shelled oats ("groats") are separated from the husks using a fan. The groats are then hoisted back to the top floor and fed through the second pair of millstones (made of French burr stone). This produces the oatmeal, which descends to the basement for bagging.<ref>[[#refZealand1992|Zealand & Zealand 1992]], pp. 6-9.</ref>

The mill is powered by the Barry Burn: there is a working dam and lade half a mile upstream, which channel water to the mill wheel. The wheel is {{convert|15|ft|6|in|m|2}} diameter, and is powered by the water dropping down from the lade on downstream side of the [[Water wheel#Overshot wheel|overshot waterwheel]] . The mill's power is controlled by a series of levers, cogs and gears in the basement. These supply power to the millstones, to the hoists, and to a fan that is used to separate the groats from the chaff.<ref>[[#refZealand1992|Zealand & Zealand 1992]], p. 5.</ref>

==History==
[[File:Barry Mill4.JPG|left|thumb|200px|The mill and its lade]]
The earliest reference to a mill on this site dates from 1539.<ref name="nts"/><ref name="Exploring">
{{cite book
  |author1=Walker, B  |author2=Ritchie, G
   |name-list-style=amp | title = Exploring Scotland's Heritage: Fife, Perthshire and Angus
  | edition = second
  | year = 1996
  | publisher = HMSO
  | location = Edinburgh
}}
</ref> Indeed, there were originally two mills on the Barry Burn, both owned by [[Balmerino Abbey]] in Fife: a corn mill ("the Nether Mill") and an oat mill ("the Over Mill"). The properties of the abbey were annexed by the crown in 1587 as a result of the [[Scottish Reformation]], and were granted to [[James Elphinstone, 1st Lord Balmerino]] in 1605.<ref>
{{cite web
  | author = James VI
  | year = 1605
  | publisher = Records of the Parliaments of Scotland
  | title = Erectioun of the abbacie of Balmirrenoch, with the landis and baroneis of Kirknewtoun and Balerno unite thairto, in ane temporall lordschip in favouris of the Lord Balmirrenoch (Erection of the abbacy of Balmerino, with the lands and baronies of Kirknewton and Balerno united thereto, in a temporal lordship in favour of [James Elphinstone, Lord Balmerino)|url = http://www.rps.ac.uk/search.php?action=fetch_jump&filename=jamesvi_trans&jump=jamesvi_m1605_6_119_d7_ms&type=trans&fragment=t1605_6_119_d7_trans
  | access-date = 2009-08-20

</ref> The mills were sold to a Robert Watson in the late 17th century and subsequently inherited by Watson's son-in-law, Robert Gardyne in the 1680s.<ref>[[#refZealand1992|Zealand & Zealand 1992]], p. 13.</ref>

Milling at the Nether Mill was discontinued and the structure, dating to 1783, is now used as a store building.<ref>{{Historic Environment Scotland|cat=PLA |num=34587 |num2=NO53SW 23 |desc=Barry, Nether Mill |access-date=8 July 2025}}</ref> In 1814, the Over Mill (which became known simply as "Barry Mill") was destroyed by a fire and the today's structure dates from its rebuilding by the owner, [[Thomas Gardyne]] of Middleton and Barry.<ref name="nts"/><ref>[[#refZealand1992|Zealand & Zealand 1992]], p. 14.</ref> The mill was purchased by the Gunn family in 1926 before being further extended in the 1930s.<ref name="nts">{{cite web|url=http://www.nts.org.uk/Property/10/|title=Barry Mill|work=[[National Trust for Scotland]] website|access-date=2009-08-18}}</ref><ref>[[#refZealand1992|Zealand & Zealand 1992]], p. 15.</ref> Barry Mill continued to produce oatmeal until the late 1970s. After that time it was used only to produce animal feed, until flood damage to the mill lade finally ended commercial operations in 1984.<ref name="Exploring" />

The derelict mill was acquired by the National Trust for Scotland in 1988,<ref name="gaz">{{cite web|url=http://www.scottish-places.info/features/featurefirst111.html |title=Barry Mill|work=Gazetteer for Scotland|access-date=2009-08-18}}</ref> and was fully restored over the next four years, to the condition it had enjoyed in 1814).<ref>[[#refZealand1992|Zealand & Zealand 1992]], pp. 17-19.</ref> It was reopened by the Trust in 1992, and has since operated on a demonstration basis. Demonstrations are offered at weekends or for parties by prior arrangement,<ref name="Exploring"/> although the mill is also operational at other times. The mill's stables have been converted into a visitor centre, and the mill itself also contains displays about the life and work of both mill and millers.<ref name="nts"/>

The mill and the nearby bridge which was part of the old road from Barry Grange to Panbride<ref name="Carnoustiepicpost1">
{{cite book
  | last = Thompson
  | first = A.L. 
  | title = Carnoustie in old picture postcards
  | year = 1998
  | publisher = European Library
  | location = Zaltbommel, Netherlands
}}
</ref> were both granted Category B [[listed building]]s status by Historic Scotland in 1971.<ref>{{Historic Environment Scotland|num=LB4649 |desc=Barry Mill including Miller's Cottage |cat=A |access-date=21 March 2019|fewer-links=yes}}</ref><ref>{{Historic Environment Scotland|num=LB4650 |desc=Upper Mill Bridge over Pitairlie Burn |cat=B |access-date=21 March 2019|fewer-links=yes}}</ref> The Nether Mill building was granted Category C listing in 1980.<ref>{{Historic Environment Scotland|num=LB4648 |desc=Nether Mill |cat=C |access-date=21 March 2019|fewer-links=yes}}</ref>

Barry Mill was granted category A listing in December 2009.<ref>{{citation|url=http://www.guideandgazette.co.uk/news/FUTURE-OF-BARRY-MILL-NOW.5901024.jp|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120804173722/http://www.guideandgazette.co.uk/news/FUTURE-OF-BARRY-MILL-NOW.5901024.jp|url-status=dead|archive-date=August 4, 2012|title=Future of Barry Mill now more secure|work=Guide and Gazette|date=December 16, 2009|access-date=December 16, 2009}}</ref>

===Closure threat===
In 2009, the mill was one of the least visited of the Trust's properties, attracting about 2,000 annual visitors.<ref name="fight">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/uk_news/scotland/tayside_and_central/7965781.stm|title=Call to fight mill closure threat |date=26 March 2009|work=[[BBC]] News website|access-date=2009-08-18}}</ref> In March 2009, the Trust, facing financial difficulties, listed the loss-making Barry Mill as one of 11 of its properties threatened with immediate closure, unless external sponsorship could be found.<ref name="closes">{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/scotland/7929328.stm|title=National Trust closes properties |date=6 March 2009|work=[[BBC]] News website|access-date=2009-08-18}}</ref> The intention was to "moth-ball" the mill until financial circumstances were better.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.guideandgazette.co.uk/news/MILL-WILL-BE-MOTHBALLED-IF.5267518.jp|title=MILL WILL BE MOTHBALLED IF IT CLOSES|last=Forsyth|first=Brian|date=14 May 2009|work=Carnoustie Guide and Gazette|access-date=2009-08-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090526063734/http://www.guideandgazette.co.uk/news/MILL-WILL-BE-MOTHBALLED-IF.5267518.jp|archive-date=26 May 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref> On 25 March, at a public meeting, "Friends of Barry Mill" was formed in an attempt to raise funds and to campaign to save the mill.<ref name="fight"/> In July 2009, the Trust announced that the property would continue to operate "for the foreseeable future" and that this was made possible due to support pledged by [[Angus Council]] and the Gibson Graham Charitable Trust.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.guideandgazette.co.uk/news/BARRY-MILL-SAVED-FROM-CLOSURE.5444791.jp|archive-url=https://archive.today/20120801061215/http://www.guideandgazette.co.uk/news/BARRY-MILL-SAVED-FROM-CLOSURE.5444791.jp|url-status=dead|archive-date=1
